issues.description: Zero-checks are scattered across every accessor instead of decomplecting the nil-or-zero concern
issues.detail: COMPLECTED. Every getter now braids three concerns: nil-receiver check, zero-value check, and the actual data access. The repeated `if f != nil { ... }` and `if !x.IsZero() { ... }` boilerplate is incidental complexity. A single helper like `raw()` returning a safe zero-shaped struct, or normalizing nil to a sentinel at construction, would put the concern in one place instead of N.

issues.description: Reflection-driven test conflates 'returns zero value' with 'behaves correctly on zero input'
issues.detail: EASY-NOT-SIMPLE. The reflective walk is familiar (one loop, all methods) but it tests a property of return types, not a property of the domain. It cannot tell you which method should return -1 vs 0 vs an empty Indexer; the `ValueNodeIndex` special case proves the design is leaking. A table of explicit (method, expected) pairs would be simpler and read as documentation.

issues.description: The real question -- why are nil *File and zero Type reachable at all -- was not asked
issues.detail: The PR description says it 'fixes panics on zero values,' but the underlying question is whether callers should ever hold a nil *File or zero Type as a valid value. Identity (the pointer/handle) and value (the IR data) are complected; making every accessor nil-safe normalizes that confusion instead of decomposing it. A constructor-enforced non-nil invariant or an explicit Optional[File] would be simpler.

issues.description: Two distinct zero concepts (nil pointer, IsZero struct) are treated as one in the API contract
issues.detail: PLACE-ORIENTED leakage. `*File` uses `f == nil`; value types use `IsZero()`. The test treats both identically, but they have different time semantics: a nil pointer is a never-constructed identity, while IsZero is a constructed-but-empty value. Naming them the same in the contract hides a real distinction callers may eventually need.

issues.description: Indexer wrappers around nil slices add a layer that hides the actual data
issues.detail: INCIDENTAL-COMPLEXITY. `seq.NewFixedSlice(nil, fn)` produces an empty Indexer rather than letting callers see a plain nil slice. The wrapper exists to make iteration uniform, but for zero values it is pure ceremony around `len == 0`. A direct slice return would be simpler and the nil-check would disappear with it.

review.summary: The PR makes accessors nil-safe by spraying `if f != nil` and `if !x.IsZero()` guards across roughly twenty methods, then proves the property with a reflective test. It works, but it treats a symptom (panics on zero) without asking the upstream question: why are nil *File and zero-valued IR nodes reachable as legitimate inputs in the first place? Identity, value, and time are complected -- a nil pointer (never-constructed identity) and an IsZero struct (constructed-but-empty value) are normalized into one contract. The reflective test is easy but not simple; the `ValueNodeIndex` special case is the tell. A constructor-enforced invariant or a single safe-raw helper would decompose the concern into one place instead of N.
